title: A tiny electrical world
text: Honeybees accumulate electric charge as they fly. Experiments show that electric fields can move their antennae and that bees can learn to associate those signals with a reward.

title: Honey’s natural chemistry
text: Honey can naturally contain small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. A bee-added enzyme called glucose oxidase helps produce it, especially when honey is diluted. The amount varies between honeys.
source: Brudzynski and colleagues · Frontiers in Microbiology, 2011

title: Two “stomachs,” two different jobs
text: Honeybees have a nectar-carrying crop, often called the honey stomach, and a separate digestive stomach. The crop lets a forager bring nectar home without sending it straight into digestion.
source: University of Arkansas Extension · About Honey Bees

title: Five eyes for a busy life
text: A honeybee has two large compound eyes and three tiny simple eyes called ocelli. The simple eyes sense light and help the bee orient itself.
source: University of Arkansas Extension · About Honey Bees

title: Four wings that work together
text: Honeybees have four wings. Tiny hooks link each hindwing to the forewing during flight, helping the pair work as one flight surface.
source: University of Arkansas Extension · About Honey Bees

title: Built-in pollen baskets
text: Worker honeybees pack pollen into special baskets on their back legs. Stiff hairs help hold the load in place for the trip back to the hive.
source: University of Arkansas Extension · About Honey Bees

title: The bees make their building material
text: Worker honeybees produce tiny wax flakes from glands beneath their abdomens. They shape that wax into the comb used to raise young bees and store food.
source: University of Arkansas Extension · About Honey Bees

title: A different kind of family tree
text: A honey bee queen usually produces daughters from fertilized eggs and sons from unfertilized eggs. Female bees have two chromosome sets; male drones have one.
source: Penn State Extension · Honey Bee Genetics Basics

title: One queen, many fathers
text: A queen mates with multiple drones, so workers in the same honey bee colony can have different fathers. A hive is a family with a surprisingly complex genetic story.
source: Penn State Extension · Honey Bee Genetics Basics

title: Royal beginnings
text: Female honey bee larvae can become queens or workers. The rich, sustained royal-jelly diet given to queen-destined larvae helps shape that remarkable difference.
source: Penn State Extension · Queen Honey Bee Development

title: A hive with air conditioning
text: Honeybees use water and wing-fanning to help cool their nest. A dependable water supply matters during hot weather.
source: Oregon State Extension · Bees in a heat wave

title: Winter is not a long nap
text: Honeybees form a heat-producing winter cluster and use stored food as fuel. The colony needs access to that food throughout cold weather.

title: Nectar and pollen do different jobs
text: Nectar provides carbohydrate energy, while pollen supplies nutrients for growing bees. Colony nutrition takes more than honey alone.

title: Honey bees are part of a bigger story
text: The western honey bee is not native to the Americas. Native bees were pollinating here long before honey bee colonies arrived with European colonists.
source: USDA ARS · History of U.S. beekeeping

title: Winter bees carry extra reserves
text: Honeybees have a nutrient-storing organ called the fat body. It becomes more developed in winter workers, helping them survive for months. Summer bees have this organ too; winter bees do not simply grow a new layer of fat.

title: How a colony shifts toward winter
text: As autumn pollen supplies decline and brood rearing slows, young workers can keep more reserves and live longer. Colony signals matter too. Foragers staying inside are not a proven single switch that turns larvae into winter bees.
source: Mattila & Otis · 2007; Smedal and colleagues · 2009; Penn State SARE GNE15-100 final report
